mcqs.question: A company deploys to production dozens of times a day and wants minimal branch ceremony. Which workflow best fits that constraint?
options: GitFlow, since its release branches provide the most control
Whichever workflow the majority of open-source projects use
A workflow with the most branch types, for maximum flexibility
Trunk-based development, since short-lived branches merged constantly match a high deploy cadence
mcqs.explanation: Trunk-based development is built specifically for continuous deployment — small changes merge to one branch constantly, with feature flags handling anything incomplete. GitFlow's release branches assume infrequent, scheduled releases, which works against a high deploy cadence, and neither popularity nor branch-type count are the relevant criteria.

mcqs.question: In GitFlow, which branch does a `hotfix/*` branch off of directly?
options: develop, since all fixes must integrate there first
main, so it can patch what's actually live without waiting for develop's other in-progress work
The most recent feature branch that touched the affected code
A dedicated staging branch separate from both main and develop
mcqs.explanation: Hotfixes branch from main precisely because production needs a fix independent of whatever unfinished work currently sits on develop; it later merges into both main and develop. It doesn't branch from develop, an arbitrary feature branch, or a separate staging branch — GitFlow defines exactly five branch roles.

mcqs.question: In trunk-based development, how does unfinished work get merged into the branch everyone deploys from without breaking production?
options: It doesn't merge until the feature is fully complete and tested
It merges into a separate long-lived integration branch first
It merges and deploys normally but stays hidden behind a feature flag until it's ready
It's merged only during a scheduled weekly release window
mcqs.explanation: Feature flags decouple merging from releasing — the code ships inert or invisible, and gets toggled on once ready, which is what lets trunk-based teams merge constantly without long-lived branches. There's no separate integration branch in this model, and merging isn't gated by a release window or by full feature completeness.

mcqs.question: A PR platform's "rebase and merge" button lands a PR's commits on main. What distinguishes this from that same platform's "squash and merge"?
options: Rebase-and-merge discards the PR's commit history; squash preserves it
They produce an identical result on main; the button is purely cosmetic
Rebase-and-merge requires manual conflict resolution first; squash never does
Rebase-and-merge replays each individual commit onto main with new hashes; squash collapses them into one new commit instead
mcqs.explanation: Rebase-and-merge keeps every commit but rewrites its hash by replaying it directly on the target branch, while squash discards the individual commits in favor of one combined commit — the opposite of what the other options claim. Both can require conflict resolution if the branch is behind, and the results are visibly different in the resulting log.

mcqs.question: Why might a team maintain a dedicated release branch even if they primarily use trunk-based development on main?
options: Release branches are required by git itself before any tag can be created
It lets them support an already-shipped version with bugfixes without needing main frozen or without shipping unrelated in-progress work
It's the only way to run CI against a specific commit
It replaces the need for feature flags entirely
mcqs.explanation: A release branch isolates a specific shipped version so it can receive fixes independently of main's ongoing changes — useful when multiple versions need parallel support. Git has no such requirement for tagging, CI can run against any commit without a dedicated branch, and it doesn't replace feature flags, which solve an unrelated problem.

mcqs.question: A team notices their feature branches routinely live for six or more weeks before merging, and every merge is painful. What's the most effective structural fix?
options: Require larger, more detailed PR descriptions to speed up review
Merge branches early and hide incomplete functionality behind feature flags, keeping the branch's actual lifetime short
Switch to a workflow with more branch types to isolate the pain
Increase the team's merge conflict resolution training
mcqs.explanation: The pain is caused by divergence time, not skill at resolving conflicts or PR documentation quality — shortening how long a branch lives before merging is what actually reduces conflict size and likelihood. Adding more branch types addresses topology, not the underlying lifespan problem, and training doesn't change how much two histories have diverged.
